title: Dot and Star Pattern Match
statement:
You get a text s and a pattern p. The pattern is made of lowercase letters and two special characters:

  • . matches any single character.
  • * means zero or more copies of the element right before it. That element is one letter or one ., never a longer chunk: ab* is a followed by any number of bs.

Return true if the pattern matches the whole text, not just part of it. Every * in p follows a letter or a .; there is never a * at the start or two in a row.

examples.why: The star repeats only the b, not "ab". The pattern means a, then any number of b's.
Both stars can take zero copies, so the pattern can match the empty text.

constraints: p holds lowercase English letters, '.' and '*'
hints: Without * this is a simple left-to-right comparison. The star is what forces a choice: how many characters should x* eat? Try reasoning about one character at a time instead of the whole count.

Let dp[i][j] say whether the first i characters of s match the first j of p. If p[j−1] is a letter or ., it must match s[i−1]. If it is *, the element before it is p[j−2]: either the star is used zero times, or it eats s[i−1] and stays available.

For a star: dp[i][j] = dp[i][j−2] or (i > 0 and p[j−2] matches s[i−1] and dp[i−1][j]). Otherwise: dp[i][j] = i > 0 and p[j−1] matches s[i−1] and dp[i−1][j−1]. Start with dp[0][0] = true; note that row 0 is not all false, because a* matches the empty text.

explain.intuition:
Let dp[i][j] be true when the first i characters of s are matched by the first j characters of p. The answer is dp[n][m], and dp[0][0] is true: an empty pattern matches an empty text. Read each cell off the last element of the pattern prefix.

If p[j−1] is a letter or ., it must consume exactly the last character of the text: s[i−1] must equal it (or it is .) and the shorter prefixes must match, dp[i−1][j−1]. If p[j−1] is *, the last element is the pair x* where x = p[j−2]. There are two cases. Zero copies: drop the pair entirely, dp[i][j−2]. One more copy: if x matches s[i−1], let the pair eat that character and stay in place, dp[i−1][j]. "Stay in place" is what lets one star eat any number of characters, one cell at a time, without ever choosing the count up front.

The zero-copies case is also why row 0 matters: dp[0][j] is true for patterns like a*, a*b* or .*, which can vanish. Forgetting that is the most common bug.
steps: Make dp of size (n + 1) × (m + 1), all false, with dp[0][0] = true.
For i from 0 to n (row 0 included) and j from 1 to m:
If p[j−1] == '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i][j−2], or, when i > 0 and p[j−2] is . or equals s[i−1], also dp[i−1][j].
Otherwise: dp[i][j] = i > 0 and (p[j−1] == '.' or p[j−1] == s[i−1]) and dp[i−1][j−1].
Return dp[n][m]. Row i reads only rows i and i − 1, so two rows are enough.
pitfalls: Treating * as repeating everything before it. ab* does not match abab.
Leaving row 0 all false except dp[0][0]. Then s = "", p = "a*" fails, and so does every match where a starred element ends up with zero copies at the start.
Testing for a substring match. s = "aa", p = "a" is false: the pattern must use up the whole text.
Matching the star greedily, as many copies as possible. s = "aaa", p = "a*a" needs the star to leave one a behind.

solutions.title: Recursion on the last pattern element
solutions.idea: Apply the recurrence directly: a star tries zero copies and one more copy, other elements must match the last text character. Without memory, several stars make the calls explode.

solutions.title: Table over text and pattern prefixes
solutions.idea: dp[i][j]: does s[0..i) match p[0..j)? A star reads dp[i][j − 2] (zero copies) and dp[i − 1][j] (eat one more character). Row 0 is filled too, for patterns that can vanish.

solutions.title: Two rows
solutions.idea: Row i reads only row i (j − 2) and row i − 1 (j and j − 1). Keep the previous row and the current one.

followups: Add + (one or more copies) and ? (zero or one copy). How does each change the star case?
Patterns are now shell globs: ? is any one character and * is any run of characters on its own. Write the recurrence.
The same pattern is tested against millions of texts. What would you build once from the pattern? (Hint: an automaton.)
